ILLUMINUS.Field.activeAlign.hint:
Which edge the lines are lined up against.

"Left" is the default and the right answer for nearly all body text: every line starts in the same place, so your eye knows where to go. "Center" suits a title or a short caption and is hard work for anything longer, since every line starts somewhere different.

"Justify" straightens both edges by stretching the spaces, which is what books do — but books also hyphenate. If you justify, turn Hyphenation on too, or you will get ugly gaps.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeAlign.label: Alignment
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeBackground.hint: Color behind the page you are reading.

ILLUMINUS.Field.activeCaps.hint:
Changes the case the lettering is drawn in, without changing what was actually typed.

"Small capitals" is the one worth knowing: every letter becomes a capital, but the ones that were lower-case are drawn shorter. It is what printed books use for the first line of a chapter, and it looks considered in a way that plain ALL CAPS does not.

Full capitals shout, and get tiring over more than a few words — fine for a short heading or a tag, poor for a paragraph.

ILLUMINUS.Field.activeEntryBorderBottomC:
What colour the bottom entry edge line is drawn in.

A line that is only slightly darker than the surface it sits on reads as a fold or a crease; one in a strong contrasting colour reads as a deliberate frame. Both are useful — just pick one on purpose.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeEntryBorderBottomS:
What kind of line the bottom entry edge is drawn as — solid, dashed, dotted, double, or one of the ridged and grooved kinds that try to look three-dimensional.

Solid is right nearly always. Dashed reads as a cut-out or a note to be filled in; double suits a formal frame around a title. The ridged ones come from very old web design and rarely look good on a printed-page style.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeEntryBorderBottomW:
How thick the bottom entry edge line is, in pixels. 0 means no line at all on that side.

You do not have to draw all four. One thick line down the left side and nothing anywhere else is the classic look for a read-aloud box, and it is quieter than a full frame.

ILLUMINUS.Field.activeEntryCornerBottomL:
How far the bottom-left corner of the entry is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeEntryCornerBottomR:

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeEntryCornerShape.h:
What kind of cut the corners of the entry are given. They all use the four sizes set above — this only changes the shape of the cut.

"Rounded" is the ordinary curve everyone expects. "Bevel" cuts the corner off flat, like a mitred picture frame or a cut gemstone — good for anything meant to look built rather than printed. "Notch" cuts a square step out of it. "Scoop" curves inward instead of outward, which makes a box look like a stamped seal or a torn ticket.

If nothing changes when you pick one, the corner sizes above are still 0 — there is no cut yet for this to shape.

ILLUMINUS.Field.activeEntryInnerShadowBl:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeEntryInnerShadowCo:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeEntryInnerShadowOf:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeEntryInnerShadowSp:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Leave it at 0 unless you have a reason. A little negative — say -2 — pulls the shadow in so it peeks out only on one side, which is a neat way to get a subtle lift without a dark halo all the way round.
Empty space below this, on the OUTSIDE of its edge — the room between it and whatever else is on the page.

This is the one people mix up with padding, so: outer spacing pushes other things away, inner spacing pushes its own contents in. If a box is crowding the paragraph above it, this is the control you want.

A negative number pulls it closer instead, which lets a box overlap what is above or below it — occasionally what you want for a heading that should sit over a banner.

ILLUMINUS.Field.activeEntryPaddingBottom:
Empty space below the entry's contents, on the INSIDE of its edge — the breathing room between the words and the border around them.

Without it, lettering sits right against the edge and looks cramped, the way text does when it runs to the very edge of a photocopy. Ten to sixteen is comfortable for a read-aloud box; a tight label might want three or four.

Not to be confused with outer spacing, which is the room *outside* the edge.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeHeadingCornerTopRi:

ILLUMINUS.Field.activeHeadingFont.hint: The typeface used for the sub-headings under a page.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeHeadingFont.label: Typeface
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeHeadingHyphens.hin:
Whether a long word may be split across two lines with a hyphen, the way a printed book does it.

It matters in narrow columns. Without hyphenation, one long word that will not fit gets pushed to the next line and the browser stretches the gaps on the line before to compensate — you end up with rivers of white space running down the page. Letting it hyphenate keeps the spacing even.

Worth turning on for anything set in columns or in a narrow box; unnecessary for full-width paragraphs, where there is room to breathe.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeHeadingInnerShadow:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Leave it at 0 unless you have a reason. A little negative — say -2 — pulls the shadow in so it peeks out only on one side, which is a neat way to get a subtle lift without a dark halo all the way round.
How tall each sub-heading row is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeHeadingMarginBotto: Space below a heading inside this box.
Empty space to the left of this, on the OUTSIDE of its edge — the room between it and whatever else is on the page.

This is the one people mix up with padding, so: outer spacing pushes other things away, inner spacing pushes its own contents in. If a box is crowding the paragraph above it, this is the control you want.

A negative number pulls it closer instead, which lets a box overlap what is above or below it — occasionally what you want for a heading that should sit over a banner.

ILLUMINUS.Field.activeHeadingMarginTop.h: Space above a heading inside this box.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeHeadingPaddingBott:
Empty space below the listed heading's name, on the INSIDE of its edge — the breathing room between the words and the border around them.

Without it, lettering sits right against the edge and looks cramped, the way text does when it runs to the very edge of a photocopy. Ten to sixteen is comfortable for a read-aloud box; a tight label might want three or four.

Not to be confused with outer spacing, which is the room *outside* the edge.

ILLUMINUS.Field.activeHeadingWrap.hint:
Lets the browser be cleverer about where the lines break, instead of simply filling each one until it runs out of room.

"Even up the lines" is for headings. A two-line heading normally comes out with eight words on the first line and one on the second; this balances them so both lines are about the same length, which looks deliberate rather than accidental.

"Avoid a lone last word" is for paragraphs. It stops a paragraph ending with a single word stranded on its own line — printers call that an orphan, and once you notice it you cannot stop noticing it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeHeadingWrap.label: Line Breaking

ILLUMINUS.Field.activeHyphens.label: Hyphenation
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeLetterSpacing.hint:
Adds space between every letter, in pixels. Negative numbers pull them together.

A little goes a very long way. Half a pixel to two pixels opens a heading out and makes it feel calm and expensive — this is what most book covers do. Five pixels makes it unreadable.

Body text almost never wants this; it is a heading and small-capitals control.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeLineHeight.hint:
How far apart the lines within a paragraph sit. It is a multiple of the text size rather than a pixel measurement, so 1.5 means one and a half times the height of the lettering.

This is the single biggest thing you can change to make a wall of text readable. 1.4 to 1.6 is comfortable for long reading; anything under 1.2 makes lines run into each other and the eye lose its place.

Headings want less than body text — around 1.1 — because their lines are short and large, and the default spacing leaves them looking disconnected. Leave it at 0 to use the page's own setting.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeLineHeight.label: Line Spacing
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeOutlineColor.hint:
What colour the outline around each letter is drawn in.

Only shows if the Outline Thickness above is more than 0. A colour close to the page's own background works best — the outline is meant to hold the letters apart from what is behind them, not to be noticed itself.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeOutlineColor.label: Outline Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeOutlineWidth.hint:
Draws a line around the outside of each letter, in pixels. 0 for none.

This is how you make pale lettering readable on top of a busy background picture: a thin dark outline separates the words from whatever is behind them, the way a subtitle on a film does.

Keep it under about 2. The outline is painted *behind* the letterform rather than over it, so it thickens the shape without eating into it — but past a certain weight it closes up the gaps in letters like e and a.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeOutlineWidth.label: Outline Thickness
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeSize.hint:
How large the lettering is, in pixels.

Leave it at 0 to use whatever the page is already using — which is usually what you want, because then everything stays in proportion if you change the page's own size later.

For body text, 14 to 17 is comfortable on a screen. Much smaller and people lean in; much larger and a paragraph stops fitting in the window.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeSize.label: Text Size

ILLUMINUS.Field.activeTextStyle.hint: How the entry for the page being read looks.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeTextStyle.label: Text Style
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeTextStyleSlant.hin:
Slants the lettering, as italics do.

It sits beside Text Style rather than inside it because the two are separate questions: you can have bold italics, light italics, or plain italics. Tick this and set Text Style to Bold and you get both.

Used on a whole read-aloud box it is the traditional way to mark text the gamemaster reads out; used on a whole page it becomes hard work to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeWeight.hint: How heavy the lettering is for the page you are reading.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeWeight.label: Current Page Thickness
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeWordSpacing.hint:
Adds space between words, on top of the ordinary gap. Negative numbers tighten them up.

Rarely needed, and easy to overdo — the eye reads groups of words, and pushing them too far apart breaks a line into a list of separate things. Occasionally useful on a short, widely letter-spaced heading, where the ordinary word gap starts to look too small by comparison.
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeWordSpacing.label: Word Spacing
ILLUMINUS.Field.activeWrap.hint:

ILLUMINUS.Field.activeWrap.label: Line Breaking
ILLUMINUS.Field.align.hint:
Which edge the lines are lined up against.

"Left" is the default and the right answer for nearly all body text: every line starts in the same place, so your eye knows where to go. "Center" suits a title or a short caption and is hard work for anything longer, since every line starts somewhere different.

"Justify" straightens both edges by stretching the spaces, which is what books do — but books also hyphenate. If you justify, turn Hyphenation on too, or you will get ugly gaps.
ILLUMINUS.Field.align.label: Alignment
ILLUMINUS.Field.alignItems.hint:
How things in a row line up top-to-bottom when they are not all the same height.

"Center" is usually right: a small tag next to a tall one will sit at its middle rather than hanging from the top. "Stretch" makes them all as tall as the tallest, which is how you get a row of boxes with matching heights even though one has more words in it. "Baseline" lines up the actual lettering, which matters when the text sizes differ.

Only does anything when Layout is set to Row.
ILLUMINUS.Field.alignItems.label: Across The Row
ILLUMINUS.Field.background.hint: The flat color behind everything else.
ILLUMINUS.Field.background.label: Fill Color

ILLUMINUS.Field.boxes.hoverInnerShadowBl:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.
ILLUMINUS.Field.boxes.hoverInnerShadowCo:

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.

A text shadow sits behind the lettering itself. Used gently it lifts words off a busy background; used hard it reads as a printing error. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.

A text shadow sits behind the lettering itself. Used gently it lifts words off a busy background; used hard it reads as a printing error. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.

A text shadow sits behind the lettering itself. Used gently it lifts words off a busy background; used hard it reads as a printing error. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.

ILLUMINUS.Field.bullet.hint:
The mark drawn in front of each item in a bulleted list.

The unusual ones are worth a look: a diamond or a dash reads quite differently from the ordinary round dot, and can tie a list to the rest of a style. "None" removes the mark entirely, which is how you make a list of items that should not look like a list — a row of trait tags, say.

ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonCornerBottomLeft.h:
How far the bottom-left corner of the button is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.
How far the bottom-right corner of the button is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonCornerShape.hint:
What kind of cut the corners of the button are given. They all use the four sizes set above — this only changes the shape of the cut.

"Rounded" is the ordinary curve everyone expects. "Bevel" cuts the corner off flat, like a mitred picture frame or a cut gemstone — good for anything meant to look built rather than printed. "Notch" cuts a square step out of it. "Scoop" curves inward instead of outward, which makes a box look like a stamped seal or a torn ticket.

If nothing changes when you pick one, the corner sizes above are still 0 — there is no cut yet for this to shape.

ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverBackground.hi: Color inside a button while the mouse is over it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverBorderColor.h: Edge color while the mouse is over a button.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverColor.hint: Text color while the mouse is over a button.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverColor.label: Text Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverTexture.hint:
A picture laid behind this — a parchment scan, a stone texture, a photograph.

Point it at any image in your Foundry data: your own art, artwork from a game system, or another module's. Leave it empty for no picture at all.

The picture sits *behind* the lettering on its own layer, so the controls under it — softness, brightness, strength — change the picture without touching the words in front of it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverTexture.label: Background Image
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverTextureAge.hi:
Browns the picture, the way an old photograph or a sheet of paper yellows with age. 0 leaves its own colours; 100 is fully sepia.

A quick way to make a modern photograph belong on a fantasy page. Try it around 60 to 80 together with Image Colour turned down.
How the picture mixes with the Fill Color behind it, rather than simply covering it up.

This is the trick that makes textures work, and it is worth learning one setting: **Multiply**. With a greyscale texture over a coloured fill, Multiply keeps every dark speck of the texture while letting the colour show through the light parts — so one grey parchment scan can be aged ivory on one style and cold slate on another, just by changing the Fill Color under it.

"Normal" means no mixing at all: the picture simply sits on top and the fill beneath it does nothing. Use that when the picture already has the colours you want.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverTextureBlur.h:
Blurs the picture before it is laid down behind the words.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverTextureBright:
Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverTextureContra:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverTextureFit.hi:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverTextureOpacit:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverTexturePositi:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonHoverTextureSatura:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonTextureContrast.hi:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonTextureFit.hint:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonTextureFit.label: Image Fit
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonTextureOpacity.hin:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.buttonTexturePosition.hi:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.
ILLUMINUS.Field.caps.hint:
Changes the case the lettering is drawn in, without changing what was actually typed.

"Small capitals" is the one worth knowing: every letter becomes a capital, but the ones that were lower-case are drawn shorter. It is what printed books use for the first line of a chapter, and it looks considered in a way that plain ALL CAPS does not.

Full capitals shout, and get tiring over more than a few words — fine for a short heading or a tag, poor for a paragraph.
ILLUMINUS.Field.caps.label: Capitals
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionAlign.hint: Which edge a caption lines up against.
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionAlign.label: Alignment
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionCaps.hint: Force capital letters in captions, or use small capitals.
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionCaps.label: Capitals
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionColor.hint: Text color of a picture's caption.
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionColor.label: Text Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionFont.hint: The typeface used for a picture's caption.
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionFont.label: Typeface
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionOutlineColor.hint:
What colour the outline around each caption letter is drawn in.

Only shows if the Outline Thickness above is more than 0. A colour close to the page's own background works best — the outline is meant to hold the letters apart from what is behind them, not to be noticed itself.
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionOutlineWidth.hint:
Draws a line around the outside of each caption letter, in pixels. 0 for none.

This is how you make pale lettering readable on top of a busy background picture: a thin dark outline separates the words from whatever is behind them, the way a subtitle on a film does.

Keep it under about 2. The outline is painted *behind* the letterform rather than over it, so it thickens the shape without eating into it — but past a certain weight it closes up the gaps in letters like e and a.
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionSide.hint: Whether the caption sits above or below the table.
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionSide.label: Caption Position
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionSize.label: Text Size
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionSpacing.hint: Space between a picture and its caption.
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionSpacing.label: Gap Above Caption
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionStyle.label: Slant
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionTextShadowBlur.hi:
A text shadow sits behind the lettering itself. Used gently it lifts words off a busy background; used hard it reads as a printing error. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionTextShadowColor.h:
A text shadow sits behind the lettering itself. Used gently it lifts words off a busy background; used hard it reads as a printing error. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionTextShadowOffsetX:
A text shadow sits behind the lettering itself. Used gently it lifts words off a busy background; used hard it reads as a printing error. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.
ILLUMINUS.Field.captionTextShadowOffsetY:
A text shadow sits behind the lettering itself. Used gently it lifts words off a busy background; used hard it reads as a printing error. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.

Slants the lettering, as italics do.

It sits beside Text Style rather than inside it because the two are separate questions: you can have bold italics, light italics, or plain italics. Tick this and set Text Style to Bold and you get both.

Used on a whole read-aloud box it is the traditional way to mark text the gamemaster reads out; used on a whole page it becomes hard work to read.

ILLUMINUS.Field.categoryBorderBottomColo:

A line that is only slightly darker than the surface it sits on reads as a fold or a crease; one in a strong contrasting colour reads as a deliberate frame. Both are useful — just pick one on purpose.
ILLUMINUS.Field.categoryBorderBottomStyl:
What kind of line the bottom category edge is drawn as — solid, dashed, dotted, double, or one of the ridged and grooved kinds that try to look three-dimensional.

Solid is right nearly always. Dashed reads as a cut-out or a note to be filled in; double suits a formal frame around a title. The ridged ones come from very old web design and rarely look good on a printed-page style.
ILLUMINUS.Field.categoryBorderBottomWidt:

You do not have to draw all four. One thick line down the left side and nothing anywhere else is the classic look for a read-aloud box, and it is quieter than a full frame.

ILLUMINUS.Field.categoryCornerBottomLeft:
How far the bottom-left corner of the category is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.

ILLUMINUS.Field.categoryCornerShape.hint:
What kind of cut the corners of the category are given. They all use the four sizes set above — this only changes the shape of the cut.

"Rounded" is the ordinary curve everyone expects. "Bevel" cuts the corner off flat, like a mitred picture frame or a cut gemstone — good for anything meant to look built rather than printed. "Notch" cuts a square step out of it. "Scoop" curves inward instead of outward, which makes a box look like a stamped seal or a torn ticket.

If nothing changes when you pick one, the corner sizes above are still 0 — there is no cut yet for this to shape.

ILLUMINUS.Field.categoryMarginBottom.hin:
Empty space below this, on the OUTSIDE of its edge — the room between it and whatever else is on the page.

This is the one people mix up with padding, so: outer spacing pushes other things away, inner spacing pushes its own contents in. If a box is crowding the paragraph above it, this is the control you want.

A negative number pulls it closer instead, which lets a box overlap what is above or below it — occasionally what you want for a heading that should sit over a banner.

ILLUMINUS.Field.codeCornerBottomLeft.hin:

ILLUMINUS.Field.codeInnerShadowBlur.hint:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeInnerShadowColor.hin:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeInnerShadowOffsetX.h:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeInnerShadowOffsetY.h:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeInnerShadowSpread.hi:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Leave it at 0 unless you have a reason. A little negative — say -2 — pulls the shadow in so it peeks out only on one side, which is a neat way to get a subtle lift without a dark halo all the way round.

ILLUMINUS.Field.codeSize.hint: How large code lettering is. 0 follows the page.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeSize.label: Text Size
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTexture.hint:
A picture laid behind this — a parchment scan, a stone texture, a photograph.

Point it at any image in your Foundry data: your own art, artwork from a game system, or another module's. Leave it empty for no picture at all.

The picture sits *behind* the lettering on its own layer, so the controls under it — softness, brightness, strength — change the picture without touching the words in front of it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTexture.label: Background Image
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureAge.hint:
Browns the picture, the way an old photograph or a sheet of paper yellows with age. 0 leaves its own colours; 100 is fully sepia.

A quick way to make a modern photograph belong on a fantasy page. Try it around 60 to 80 together with Image Colour turned down.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureAge.label: Image Age
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureBlend.hint:
How the picture mixes with the Fill Color behind it, rather than simply covering it up.

This is the trick that makes textures work, and it is worth learning one setting: **Multiply**. With a greyscale texture over a coloured fill, Multiply keeps every dark speck of the texture while letting the colour show through the light parts — so one grey parchment scan can be aged ivory on one style and cold slate on another, just by changing the Fill Color under it.

"Normal" means no mixing at all: the picture simply sits on top and the fill beneath it does nothing. Use that when the picture already has the colours you want.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureBlend.label: Image Blending
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureBlur.hint:
Blurs the picture before it is laid down behind the words.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureBlur.label: Image Softness
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureBrightness.hi:
Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureContrast.hint:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureFit.hint:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureFit.label: Image Fit
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureOpacity.hint:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureOpacity.label: Image Strength
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTexturePosition.hint:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.codeTextureSaturation.hi:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.

The picture sits *behind* the lettering on its own layer, so the controls under it — softness, brightness, strength — change the picture without touching the words in front of it.

ILLUMINUS.Field.dropdownTextureAge.hint:
Browns the picture, the way an old photograph or a sheet of paper yellows with age. 0 leaves its own colours; 100 is fully sepia.

A quick way to make a modern photograph belong on a fantasy page. Try it around 60 to 80 together with Image Colour turned down.
ILLUMINUS.Field.dropdownTextureAge.label: Image Age
ILLUMINUS.Field.dropdownTextureBlend.hin:
How the picture mixes with the Fill Color behind it, rather than simply covering it up.

This is the trick that makes textures work, and it is worth learning one setting: **Multiply**. With a greyscale texture over a coloured fill, Multiply keeps every dark speck of the texture while letting the colour show through the light parts — so one grey parchment scan can be aged ivory on one style and cold slate on another, just by changing the Fill Color under it.

"Normal" means no mixing at all: the picture simply sits on top and the fill beneath it does nothing. Use that when the picture already has the colours you want.
ILLUMINUS.Field.dropdownTextureBlur.hint:
Blurs the picture before it is laid down behind the words.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.
ILLUMINUS.Field.dropdownTextureBrightnes:
Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.dropdownTextureFit.hint:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.dropdownTextureFit.label: Image Fit
ILLUMINUS.Field.dropdownTextureOpacity.h:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.dropdownTextureSaturatio:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.
ILLUMINUS.Field.editor.headerButtonInner:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Leave it at 0 unless you have a reason. A little negative — say -2 — pulls the shadow in so it peeks out only on one side, which is a neat way to get a subtle lift without a dark halo all the way round.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.

ILLUMINUS.Field.entryActiveBackground.hi: The color behind the page being read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryActiveTexture.hint:
A picture laid behind this — a parchment scan, a stone texture, a photograph.

Point it at any image in your Foundry data: your own art, artwork from a game system, or another module's. Leave it empty for no picture at all.

The picture sits *behind* the lettering on its own layer, so the controls under it — softness, brightness, strength — change the picture without touching the words in front of it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryActiveTexture.label: Background Image
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryActiveTextureAge.hi:
Browns the picture, the way an old photograph or a sheet of paper yellows with age. 0 leaves its own colours; 100 is fully sepia.

A quick way to make a modern photograph belong on a fantasy page. Try it around 60 to 80 together with Image Colour turned down.
How the picture mixes with the Fill Color behind it, rather than simply covering it up.

This is the trick that makes textures work, and it is worth learning one setting: **Multiply**. With a greyscale texture over a coloured fill, Multiply keeps every dark speck of the texture while letting the colour show through the light parts — so one grey parchment scan can be aged ivory on one style and cold slate on another, just by changing the Fill Color under it.

ILLUMINUS.Field.entryActiveTextureBlur.h:
Blurs the picture before it is laid down behind the words.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryActiveTextureBright:
Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryActiveTextureContra:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryActiveTextureFit.hi:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryActiveTextureOpacit:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryActiveTexturePositi:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryActiveTextureSatura:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryBackground.hint: The color behind a listed page.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryBackground.label: Fill Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryBorderBottomColor.h:
What colour the bottom entry edge line is drawn in.

A line that is only slightly darker than the surface it sits on reads as a fold or a crease; one in a strong contrasting colour reads as a deliberate frame. Both are useful — just pick one on purpose.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryBorderBottomStyle.h:
What kind of line the bottom entry edge is drawn as — solid, dashed, dotted, double, or one of the ridged and grooved kinds that try to look three-dimensional.

Solid is right nearly always. Dashed reads as a cut-out or a note to be filled in; double suits a formal frame around a title. The ridged ones come from very old web design and rarely look good on a printed-page style.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryBorderBottomWidth.h:
How thick the bottom entry edge line is, in pixels. 0 means no line at all on that side.

You do not have to draw all four. One thick line down the left side and nothing anywhere else is the classic look for a read-aloud box, and it is quieter than a full frame.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryTexturePosition.hin:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.entryTextureSaturation.h:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldBackground.hint: The color behind a setting's box.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldBackground.label: Fill Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldBorderBottomColor.h:
What colour the bottom field edge line is drawn in.

A line that is only slightly darker than the surface it sits on reads as a fold or a crease; one in a strong contrasting colour reads as a deliberate frame. Both are useful — just pick one on purpose.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldBorderBottomStyle.h:
What kind of line the bottom field edge is drawn as — solid, dashed, dotted, double, or one of the ridged and grooved kinds that try to look three-dimensional.

Solid is right nearly always. Dashed reads as a cut-out or a note to be filled in; double suits a formal frame around a title. The ridged ones come from very old web design and rarely look good on a printed-page style.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldBorderBottomWidth.h:
How thick the bottom field edge line is, in pixels. 0 means no line at all on that side.

You do not have to draw all four. One thick line down the left side and nothing anywhere else is the classic look for a read-aloud box, and it is quieter than a full frame.

ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCheckColor.hint: Color of the empty box. Leave empty to keep the one Foundry draws.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCheckColor.label: Tick Box Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCheckMarkColor.hint: Color of the tick inside the box.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCheckSize.hint: How large the box is drawn. 0 leaves it the size Foundry draws it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCheckSize.label: Tick Box Size
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCheckTickedColor.hi: Color the box turns once it is ticked.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldColor.label: Text Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCornerBottomLeft.hi:
How far the bottom-left corner of the field is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCornerBottomRight.h:
How far the bottom-right corner of the field is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCornerShape.hint:
What kind of cut the corners of the field are given. They all use the four sizes set above — this only changes the shape of the cut.

"Rounded" is the ordinary curve everyone expects. "Bevel" cuts the corner off flat, like a mitred picture frame or a cut gemstone — good for anything meant to look built rather than printed. "Notch" cuts a square step out of it. "Scoop" curves inward instead of outward, which makes a box look like a stamped seal or a torn ticket.

If nothing changes when you pick one, the corner sizes above are still 0 — there is no cut yet for this to shape.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCornerShape.label: Corner Shape
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCornerTopLeft.hint:
How far the top-left corner of the field is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCornerTopLeft.label: Top-Left Corner
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldCornerTopRight.hint:
How far the top-right corner of the field is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldFont.hint: The lettering on the settings above the editing controls.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldFont.label: Typeface
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldInnerShadowBlur.hin:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldInnerShadowColor.hi:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldInnerShadowSpread.h:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Leave it at 0 unless you have a reason. A little negative — say -2 — pulls the shadow in so it peeks out only on one side, which is a neat way to get a subtle lift without a dark halo all the way round.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldOutlineColor.hint:
What colour the outline around each letter is drawn in.

Only shows if the Outline Thickness above is more than 0. A colour close to the page's own background works best — the outline is meant to hold the letters apart from what is behind them, not to be noticed itself.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldOutlineColor.label: Outline Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldOutlineWidth.hint:
Draws a line around the outside of each letter, in pixels. 0 for none.

This is how you make pale lettering readable on top of a busy background picture: a thin dark outline separates the words from whatever is behind them, the way a subtitle on a film does.

Keep it under about 2. The outline is painted *behind* the letterform rather than over it, so it thickens the shape without eating into it — but past a certain weight it closes up the gaps in letters like e and a.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldOutlineWidth.label: Outline Thickness
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldPaddingBottom.hint:
Empty space below the field's contents, on the INSIDE of its edge — the breathing room between the words and the border around them.

Without it, lettering sits right against the edge and looks cramped, the way text does when it runs to the very edge of a photocopy. Ten to sixteen is comfortable for a read-aloud box; a tight label might want three or four.

Not to be confused with outer spacing, which is the room *outside* the edge.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldPaddingBottom.label: Bottom Padding
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldPaddingLeft.hint:
Empty space to the left of the field's contents, on the INSIDE of its edge — the breathing room between the words and the border around them.

Without it, lettering sits right against the edge and looks cramped, the way text does when it runs to the very edge of a photocopy. Ten to sixteen is comfortable for a read-aloud box; a tight label might want three or four.

Not to be confused with outer spacing, which is the room *outside* the edge.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldPaddingLeft.label: Left Padding
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldPaddingRight.hint:
Empty space to the right of the field's contents, on the INSIDE of its edge — the breathing room between the words and the border around them.

Without it, lettering sits right against the edge and looks cramped, the way text does when it runs to the very edge of a photocopy. Ten to sixteen is comfortable for a read-aloud box; a tight label might want three or four.

Not to be confused with outer spacing, which is the room *outside* the edge.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldPaddingRight.label: Right Padding
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldPaddingTop.hint:
Empty space above the field's contents, on the INSIDE of its edge — the breathing room between the words and the border around them.

Without it, lettering sits right against the edge and looks cramped, the way text does when it runs to the very edge of a photocopy. Ten to sixteen is comfortable for a read-aloud box; a tight label might want three or four.

Not to be confused with outer spacing, which is the room *outside* the edge.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldPaddingTop.label: Top Padding
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldShadowBlur.hint:
A shadow is what makes something look raised off the page rather than printed flat on it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldShadowBlur.label: Softness
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldShadowColor.hint:
A shadow is what makes something look raised off the page rather than printed flat on it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldShadowColor.label: Color

A shadow is what makes something look raised off the page rather than printed flat on it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldShadowOffsetX.label: Horizontal Offset
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldShadowOffsetY.hint:
A shadow is what makes something look raised off the page rather than printed flat on it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldShadowOffsetY.label: Vertical Offset
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldShadowSpread.hint:

ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldShadowSpread.label: Size
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldSize.hint: How large those settings are drawn. 0 follows the window.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldSize.label: Text Size
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextShadowBlur.hint:
A text shadow sits behind the lettering itself. Used gently it lifts words off a busy background; used hard it reads as a printing error. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.

A text shadow sits behind the lettering itself. Used gently it lifts words off a busy background; used hard it reads as a printing error. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.

ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextStyle.hint: How the field lettering looks — its weight and whether it is italic.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextStyle.label: Text Style
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextStyleSlant.hint:
Slants the lettering, as italics do.

It sits beside Text Style rather than inside it because the two are separate questions: you can have bold italics, light italics, or plain italics. Tick this and set Text Style to Bold and you get both.

Used on a whole read-aloud box it is the traditional way to mark text the gamemaster reads out; used on a whole page it becomes hard work to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTexture.hint:
A picture laid behind this — a parchment scan, a stone texture, a photograph.

Point it at any image in your Foundry data: your own art, artwork from a game system, or another module's. Leave it empty for no picture at all.

The picture sits *behind* the lettering on its own layer, so the controls under it — softness, brightness, strength — change the picture without touching the words in front of it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTexture.label: Background Image
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextureAge.hint:
Browns the picture, the way an old photograph or a sheet of paper yellows with age. 0 leaves its own colours; 100 is fully sepia.

A quick way to make a modern photograph belong on a fantasy page. Try it around 60 to 80 together with Image Colour turned down.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextureAge.label: Image Age
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextureBlend.hint:
How the picture mixes with the Fill Color behind it, rather than simply covering it up.

This is the trick that makes textures work, and it is worth learning one setting: **Multiply**. With a greyscale texture over a coloured fill, Multiply keeps every dark speck of the texture while letting the colour show through the light parts — so one grey parchment scan can be aged ivory on one style and cold slate on another, just by changing the Fill Color under it.

"Normal" means no mixing at all: the picture simply sits on top and the fill beneath it does nothing. Use that when the picture already has the colours you want.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextureBlend.label: Image Blending
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextureBlur.hint:
Blurs the picture before it is laid down behind the words.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextureBlur.label: Image Softness
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextureBrightness.h:
Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextureContrast.hin:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextureFit.hint:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextureFit.label: Image Fit
ILLUMINUS.Field.fieldTextureOpacity.hint:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
