ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTextStyle.hint: How the hover field lettering looks — its weight and whether it is italic.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTextStyleSlant:
Slants the lettering, as italics do.

It sits beside Text Style rather than inside it because the two are separate questions: you can have bold italics, light italics, or plain italics. Tick this and set Text Style to Bold and you get both.

Used on a whole read-aloud box it is the traditional way to mark text the gamemaster reads out; used on a whole page it becomes hard work to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTexture.hint:
A picture laid behind this — a parchment scan, a stone texture, a photograph.

Point it at any image in your Foundry data: your own art, artwork from a game system, or another module's. Leave it empty for no picture at all.

The picture sits *behind* the lettering on its own layer, so the controls under it — softness, brightness, strength — change the picture without touching the words in front of it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTexture.label: Background Image
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTextureAge.hin:
Browns the picture, the way an old photograph or a sheet of paper yellows with age. 0 leaves its own colours; 100 is fully sepia.

A quick way to make a modern photograph belong on a fantasy page. Try it around 60 to 80 together with Image Colour turned down.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTextureBlend.h:
How the picture mixes with the Fill Color behind it, rather than simply covering it up.

This is the trick that makes textures work, and it is worth learning one setting: **Multiply**. With a greyscale texture over a coloured fill, Multiply keeps every dark speck of the texture while letting the colour show through the light parts — so one grey parchment scan can be aged ivory on one style and cold slate on another, just by changing the Fill Color under it.

"Normal" means no mixing at all: the picture simply sits on top and the fill beneath it does nothing. Use that when the picture already has the colours you want.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTextureBlur.hi:
Blurs the picture before it is laid down behind the words.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTextureBrightn:
Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTextureContras:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTextureFit.hin:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTextureOpacity:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTexturePositio:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFieldTextureSaturat:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFirstLineIndent.hin:
Pushes the first line of every paragraph inward, the way a printed novel does.

It is the traditional alternative to leaving a blank line between paragraphs — books use one or the other, rarely both. If your paragraphs already have clear space between them, this will look like a mistake.

Around 16 to 24 is the usual amount. The very first paragraph after a heading is left alone, as it should be.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFlexDirection.hint:
Which way a row runs: left to right as you would expect, or reversed, or turned on its side to run down the page.

Reversed is more useful than it sounds — it flips the order without you having to retype anything, so a rarity tag can be made to sit at the end of a line that was written with it at the start.

Only does anything when Layout is set to Row.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFlexDirection.label: Row Direction
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFlexWrap.hint:
What happens when a row has more in it than fits across the page: everything is squashed onto one line, or the overflow drops onto a second line beneath.

Let it wrap for anything whose length you do not control — a list of traits on a monster might be three items or fifteen. Keep it on one line only when you know it is short and want it to stay put.

Only does anything when Layout is set to Row.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFlexWrap.label: Row Wrapping
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFlip.hint: Flip the picture, so an illustration can face into the page.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFlip.label: Mirror
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFloat.hint:
Lets the text of the page flow around this instead of stopping for it.

Floated left, the box sits against the left margin and the paragraphs wrap down its right-hand side — exactly how a printed adventure sets a sidebar or a portrait. Without it the box takes the full width and the text starts again underneath.

Set a Width below as well, or there is no room left for the text to wrap into.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFloat.label: Float
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldColor.hint: Color of the marker. Leave empty to follow the lettering beside it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldColor.label: Marker Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldGap.hint: Space between the marker and the words beside it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldGap.label: Marker Gap
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldIcon.hint: The shape of the marker a reader clicks to fold.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldIcon.label: Marker
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldShown.hint: Whether a marker appears for folding this away. A reader clicks it to hide what is under it and clicks again to bring it back; nothing is saved, so a page opens as its author left it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldShown.label: Can Be Folded
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldSize.hint: How large the marker is. 0 follows the lettering beside it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldSize.label: Marker Size
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldTurn.hint: How far the marker turns when what it holds is open. 90 points a sideways arrow downwards.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFoldTurn.label: Marker Turn
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFont.hint:
Which lettering this is set in.

The list is whatever Foundry knows about, so to add your own — a proper display face for chapter openings, say — install it under Foundry's Configure Font Families menu and it will appear here.

Two typefaces on a page is plenty: one with character for headings, one plain and comfortable for the body. Three or more starts to look like a ransom note.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFont.label: Typeface
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFrameMaxWidth.hint: The widest the window may be drawn, however far it is dragged out. 0 lets Foundry decide.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFrameMaxWidth.label: Maximum Width
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFrameMinWidth.hint: The narrowest the window may be drawn, however far it is dragged in. 0 lets Foundry decide.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFrameMinWidth.label: Minimum Width
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFrost.hint:
Blurs whatever sits behind this, the way frosted bathroom glass blurs what is on the other side of it.

It only shows if the fill in front of it is partly see-through — behind a solid colour there is nothing to see. So this works together with the Fill Color's opacity: drop the fill to something like 60% and then frost what is behind it, and you get a panel that feels like glass laid over the page rather than a hole cut in it.

0 turns it off entirely. Six to twelve is usually enough — heavy blurring costs the browser real work on every frame.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverFrost.label: Frosting
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGap.hint:
How much space to leave between the things inside a row, in pixels.

Simpler than putting outer spacing on each one, because it only goes *between* them and not around the outside. Six to ten pixels usually separates a line of tags without them drifting apart.

Only does anything when Layout is set to Row.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGap.label: Gap Between
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGlowColor.hint: A glow that follows the picture's own edges, not its box. Fully transparent means none.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGlowColor.label: Glow Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGlowOffsetX.hint: How far the glow sits to the right. Negative moves it left.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGlowOffsetX.label: Glow Horizontal Offset
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGlowOffsetY.hint: How far the glow sits below. Negative moves it up.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGlowOffsetY.label: Glow Vertical Offset
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGlowSize.hint: How far the glow spreads. 0 draws nothing.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGlowSize.label: Glow Size
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGradientAngle.hint:
Which way the fade runs, as an angle in degrees.

180 runs from the top down, which is the usual one — it reads as light falling from above. 90 runs from the left across. 0 runs from the bottom up, and 135 runs diagonally.

If you cannot see any fade at all, the two colours above are probably still transparent.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGradientAngle.label: Graduated Direction
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGradientFrom.hint:
Fades the fill from one colour into another across the shape, instead of one flat colour throughout. This is the colour it starts at.

Both ends start fully transparent, which means no fade at all — so nothing happens until you set both this and Graduated To.

Keep the two colours close together. A parchment that fades from cream to a slightly deeper cream looks like real paper catching the light; one that fades from yellow to purple looks like a website from 1998.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGradientFrom.label: Graduated From
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGradientTo.hint:
The colour the fill fades into, at the far end of the direction set below.

Leave both this and Graduated From fully transparent for an ordinary flat fill.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverGradientTo.label: Graduated To
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderAlign.hint: Which edge the top row's text lines up against.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderAlign.label: Alignment
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderBackground.hi: Background of the top row of a table.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderButtonBorderB:
What colour the bottom button edge line is drawn in.

A line that is only slightly darker than the surface it sits on reads as a fold or a crease; one in a strong contrasting colour reads as a deliberate frame. Both are useful — just pick one on purpose.

What kind of line the bottom button edge is drawn as — solid, dashed, dotted, double, or one of the ridged and grooved kinds that try to look three-dimensional.

Solid is right nearly always. Dashed reads as a cut-out or a note to be filled in; double suits a formal frame around a title. The ridged ones come from very old web design and rarely look good on a printed-page style.

How thick the bottom button edge line is, in pixels. 0 means no line at all on that side.

You do not have to draw all four. One thick line down the left side and nothing anywhere else is the classic look for a read-aloud box, and it is quieter than a full frame.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderButtonCornerB:
How far the bottom-left corner of the button is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.

How far the bottom-right corner of the button is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderButtonCornerS:
What kind of cut the corners of the button are given. They all use the four sizes set above — this only changes the shape of the cut.

"Rounded" is the ordinary curve everyone expects. "Bevel" cuts the corner off flat, like a mitred picture frame or a cut gemstone — good for anything meant to look built rather than printed. "Notch" cuts a square step out of it. "Scoop" curves inward instead of outward, which makes a box look like a stamped seal or a torn ticket.

If nothing changes when you pick one, the corner sizes above are still 0 — there is no cut yet for this to shape.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderButtonInnerSh:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Leave it at 0 unless you have a reason. A little negative — say -2 — pulls the shadow in so it peeks out only on one side, which is a neat way to get a subtle lift without a dark halo all the way round.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderLetterSpacing: Extra space between letters in the top row.
What colour the outline around each header letter is drawn in.

Only shows if the Outline Thickness above is more than 0. A colour close to the page's own background works best — the outline is meant to hold the letters apart from what is behind them, not to be noticed itself.
Draws a line around the outside of each header letter, in pixels. 0 for none.

This is how you make pale lettering readable on top of a busy background picture: a thin dark outline separates the words from whatever is behind them, the way a subtitle on a film does.

Keep it under about 2. The outline is painted *behind* the letterform rather than over it, so it thickens the shape without eating into it — but past a certain weight it closes up the gaps in letters like e and a.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTextStyle.hin: How the hover header lettering looks — its weight and whether it is italic.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTextStyleSlan:
Slants the lettering, as italics do.

It sits beside Text Style rather than inside it because the two are separate questions: you can have bold italics, light italics, or plain italics. Tick this and set Text Style to Bold and you get both.

Used on a whole read-aloud box it is the traditional way to mark text the gamemaster reads out; used on a whole page it becomes hard work to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTexture.hint:
A picture laid behind this — a parchment scan, a stone texture, a photograph.

Point it at any image in your Foundry data: your own art, artwork from a game system, or another module's. Leave it empty for no picture at all.

The picture sits *behind* the lettering on its own layer, so the controls under it — softness, brightness, strength — change the picture without touching the words in front of it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTexture.label: Background Image
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTextureAge.hi:
Browns the picture, the way an old photograph or a sheet of paper yellows with age. 0 leaves its own colours; 100 is fully sepia.

A quick way to make a modern photograph belong on a fantasy page. Try it around 60 to 80 together with Image Colour turned down.
How the picture mixes with the Fill Color behind it, rather than simply covering it up.

This is the trick that makes textures work, and it is worth learning one setting: **Multiply**. With a greyscale texture over a coloured fill, Multiply keeps every dark speck of the texture while letting the colour show through the light parts — so one grey parchment scan can be aged ivory on one style and cold slate on another, just by changing the Fill Color under it.

"Normal" means no mixing at all: the picture simply sits on top and the fill beneath it does nothing. Use that when the picture already has the colours you want.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTextureBlur.h:
Blurs the picture before it is laid down behind the words.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTextureBright:
Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTextureContra:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTextureFit.hi:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTextureOpacit:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTexturePositi:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeaderTextureSatura:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingFont.hint: The typeface used for the sub-headings under a page.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingFont.label: Typeface
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingHyphens.hint:
Whether a long word may be split across two lines with a hyphen, the way a printed book does it.

It matters in narrow columns. Without hyphenation, one long word that will not fit gets pushed to the next line and the browser stretches the gaps on the line before to compensate — you end up with rivers of white space running down the page. Letting it hyphenate keeps the spacing even.

Worth turning on for anything set in columns or in a narrow box; unnecessary for full-width paragraphs, where there is room to breathe.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingIndent.hint: How far the sub-headings are pushed in from the left.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingIndent.label: Indent
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingInnerShadowB:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingInnerShadowC:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingInnerShadowO:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingInnerShadowS:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Leave it at 0 unless you have a reason. A little negative — say -2 — pulls the shadow in so it peeks out only on one side, which is a neat way to get a subtle lift without a dark halo all the way round.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingLineHeight.h: How tall each sub-heading row is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingMarginBottom: Space below a heading inside this box.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingMarginLeft.h:
Empty space to the left of this, on the OUTSIDE of its edge — the room between it and whatever else is on the page.

This is the one people mix up with padding, so: outer spacing pushes other things away, inner spacing pushes its own contents in. If a box is crowding the paragraph above it, this is the control you want.

A negative number pulls it closer instead, which lets a box overlap what is above or below it — occasionally what you want for a heading that should sit over a banner.
Empty space to the right of this, on the OUTSIDE of its edge — the room between it and whatever else is on the page.

This is the one people mix up with padding, so: outer spacing pushes other things away, inner spacing pushes its own contents in. If a box is crowding the paragraph above it, this is the control you want.

A negative number pulls it closer instead, which lets a box overlap what is above or below it — occasionally what you want for a heading that should sit over a banner.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingMarginTop.hi: Space above a heading inside this box.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingOutlineColor:
What colour the outline around each heading letter is drawn in.

Only shows if the Outline Thickness above is more than 0. A colour close to the page's own background works best — the outline is meant to hold the letters apart from what is behind them, not to be noticed itself.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingOutlineWidth:
Draws a line around the outside of each heading letter, in pixels. 0 for none.

This is how you make pale lettering readable on top of a busy background picture: a thin dark outline separates the words from whatever is behind them, the way a subtitle on a film does.

Keep it under about 2. The outline is painted *behind* the letterform rather than over it, so it thickens the shape without eating into it — but past a certain weight it closes up the gaps in letters like e and a.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingPaddingBotto:

Without it, lettering sits right against the edge and looks cramped, the way text does when it runs to the very edge of a photocopy. Ten to sixteen is comfortable for a read-aloud box; a tight label might want three or four.

Not to be confused with outer spacing, which is the room *outside* the edge.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingTextStyle.hi: How the hover heading lettering looks — its weight and whether it is italic.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingTextStyleSla:
Slants the lettering, as italics do.

It sits beside Text Style rather than inside it because the two are separate questions: you can have bold italics, light italics, or plain italics. Tick this and set Text Style to Bold and you get both.

Used on a whole read-aloud box it is the traditional way to mark text the gamemaster reads out; used on a whole page it becomes hard work to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingTexture.hint:
A picture laid behind this — a parchment scan, a stone texture, a photograph.

Point it at any image in your Foundry data: your own art, artwork from a game system, or another module's. Leave it empty for no picture at all.

The picture sits *behind* the lettering on its own layer, so the controls under it — softness, brightness, strength — change the picture without touching the words in front of it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingTextureAge.h:
Browns the picture, the way an old photograph or a sheet of paper yellows with age. 0 leaves its own colours; 100 is fully sepia.

A quick way to make a modern photograph belong on a fantasy page. Try it around 60 to 80 together with Image Colour turned down.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingTextureBlend:
How the picture mixes with the Fill Color behind it, rather than simply covering it up.

This is the trick that makes textures work, and it is worth learning one setting: **Multiply**. With a greyscale texture over a coloured fill, Multiply keeps every dark speck of the texture while letting the colour show through the light parts — so one grey parchment scan can be aged ivory on one style and cold slate on another, just by changing the Fill Color under it.

"Normal" means no mixing at all: the picture simply sits on top and the fill beneath it does nothing. Use that when the picture already has the colours you want.
Blurs the picture before it is laid down behind the words.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingTextureBrigh:
Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingTextureContr:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingTextureFit.h:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingTextureOpaci:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingTexturePosit:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingTextureSatur:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingWrap.hint:
Lets the browser be cleverer about where the lines break, instead of simply filling each one until it runs out of room.

"Even up the lines" is for headings. A two-line heading normally comes out with eight words on the first line and one on the second; this balances them so both lines are about the same length, which looks deliberate rather than accidental.

"Avoid a lone last word" is for paragraphs. It stops a paragraph ending with a single word stranded on its own line — printers call that an orphan, and once you notice it you cannot stop noticing it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverHeadingWrap.label: Line Breaking

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverJustify.hint:
Where the spare room in a row goes, once everything in it has been placed.

"Start" bunches everything to the left and leaves the gap at the end. "Space between" pushes the first thing hard left and the last hard right with the gap shared out in the middle — which is how you get a name on the left and a level on the right of the same line. "Center" gathers everything in the middle with the gap split either side.

Only does anything when Layout is set to Row.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverJustify.label: Along The Row
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverLetterSpacing.hint:
Adds space between every letter, in pixels. Negative numbers pull them together.

A little goes a very long way. Half a pixel to two pixels opens a heading out and makes it feel calm and expensive — this is what most book covers do. Five pixels makes it unreadable.

Body text almost never wants this; it is a heading and small-capitals control.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverLetterSpacing.label: Letter Spacing
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverLift.hint:
Nudges the tag up or down from the line of text it sits in, without moving the line itself.

Useful because a tag with padding and a background often looks like it is sitting slightly too low next to the words around it. A pixel or two up usually settles it. Negative numbers push it down.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverLift.label: Lift
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverLineHeight.hint:
How far apart the lines within a paragraph sit. It is a multiple of the text size rather than a pixel measurement, so 1.5 means one and a half times the height of the lettering.

This is the single biggest thing you can change to make a wall of text readable. 1.4 to 1.6 is comfortable for long reading; anything under 1.2 makes lines run into each other and the eye lose its place.

Headings want less than body text — around 1.1 — because their lines are short and large, and the default spacing leaves them looking disconnected. Leave it at 0 to use the page's own setting.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverLineHeight.label: Line Spacing

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListBorderBottomCol:
What colour the bottom list edge line is drawn in.

A line that is only slightly darker than the surface it sits on reads as a fold or a crease; one in a strong contrasting colour reads as a deliberate frame. Both are useful — just pick one on purpose.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListBorderBottomSty:
What kind of line the bottom list edge is drawn as — solid, dashed, dotted, double, or one of the ridged and grooved kinds that try to look three-dimensional.

Solid is right nearly always. Dashed reads as a cut-out or a note to be filled in; double suits a formal frame around a title. The ridged ones come from very old web design and rarely look good on a printed-page style.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListBorderBottomWid:
How thick the bottom list edge line is, in pixels. 0 means no line at all on that side.

You do not have to draw all four. One thick line down the left side and nothing anywhere else is the classic look for a read-aloud box, and it is quieter than a full frame.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListCornerBottomLef:
How far the bottom-left corner of the list is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListCornerShape.hin:
What kind of cut the corners of the list are given. They all use the four sizes set above — this only changes the shape of the cut.

"Rounded" is the ordinary curve everyone expects. "Bevel" cuts the corner off flat, like a mitred picture frame or a cut gemstone — good for anything meant to look built rather than printed. "Notch" cuts a square step out of it. "Scoop" curves inward instead of outward, which makes a box look like a stamped seal or a torn ticket.

If nothing changes when you pick one, the corner sizes above are still 0 — there is no cut yet for this to shape.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListInnerShadowBlur:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListInnerShadowColo:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListInnerShadowOffs:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListInnerShadowSpre:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Leave it at 0 unless you have a reason. A little negative — say -2 — pulls the shadow in so it peeks out only on one side, which is a neat way to get a subtle lift without a dark halo all the way round.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListPaddingBottom.h:
Empty space below the entries, on the INSIDE of its edge — the breathing room between the words and the border around them.

Without it, lettering sits right against the edge and looks cramped, the way text does when it runs to the very edge of a photocopy. Ten to sixteen is comfortable for a read-aloud box; a tight label might want three or four.

Not to be confused with outer spacing, which is the room *outside* the edge.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListTexture.hint:
A picture laid behind this — a parchment scan, a stone texture, a photograph.

Point it at any image in your Foundry data: your own art, artwork from a game system, or another module's. Leave it empty for no picture at all.

The picture sits *behind* the lettering on its own layer, so the controls under it — softness, brightness, strength — change the picture without touching the words in front of it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListTexture.label: Background Image
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListTextureAge.hint:
Browns the picture, the way an old photograph or a sheet of paper yellows with age. 0 leaves its own colours; 100 is fully sepia.

A quick way to make a modern photograph belong on a fantasy page. Try it around 60 to 80 together with Image Colour turned down.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListTextureBlend.hi:
How the picture mixes with the Fill Color behind it, rather than simply covering it up.

This is the trick that makes textures work, and it is worth learning one setting: **Multiply**. With a greyscale texture over a coloured fill, Multiply keeps every dark speck of the texture while letting the colour show through the light parts — so one grey parchment scan can be aged ivory on one style and cold slate on another, just by changing the Fill Color under it.

"Normal" means no mixing at all: the picture simply sits on top and the fill beneath it does nothing. Use that when the picture already has the colours you want.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListTextureBlur.hin:
Blurs the picture before it is laid down behind the words.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListTextureBrightne:
Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListTextureContrast:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListTextureFit.hint:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListTexturePosition:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverListTextureSaturati:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverMarginBottom.hint:
Empty space below this, on the OUTSIDE of its edge — the room between it and whatever else is on the page.

This is the one people mix up with padding, so: outer spacing pushes other things away, inner spacing pushes its own contents in. If a box is crowding the paragraph above it, this is the control you want.

A negative number pulls it closer instead, which lets a box overlap what is above or below it — occasionally what you want for a heading that should sit over a banner.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverMarginBottom.label: Bottom Gap

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverMarkerSize.hint: How large bullets and item numbers are. 0 follows the text.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverMaxHeight.hint:

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverMaxHeight.label: Most Height
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverMaxWidth.hint: Stops lines growing too long to read comfortably. Set to 0 for no limit.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOffsetLeft.hint:
Moves this to the right of where the page put it, in pixels. A negative number moves it left.

As with Nudge Down, nothing moves out of the way — it just slides, and can overlap its neighbours. A few pixels either way is usually all you want; large numbers push things off the page entirely.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOffsetLeft.label: Nudge Right
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOffsetTop.hint:
Moves this down from where the page put it, in pixels. A negative number moves it up instead.

Nothing else shifts to make room — it simply slides, and may end up overlapping what is above or below. That is the point: it is how you get a heading to sit slightly over a banner, or lift a tag to line up with the words beside it.

When How It Sits is set to "Held in view", this means something different: it is how far below the top of the page the thing comes to rest.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOffsetTop.label: Nudge Down
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOpacity.hint: How solid the picture is. Lower values let the page show through.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOpacity.label: Opacity
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOutlineColor.hint:
What colour the outline around each letter is drawn in.

Only shows if the Outline Thickness above is more than 0. A colour close to the page's own background works best — the outline is meant to hold the letters apart from what is behind them, not to be noticed itself.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOutlineColor.label: Outline Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOutlineWidth.hint:
Draws a line around the outside of each letter, in pixels. 0 for none.

This is how you make pale lettering readable on top of a busy background picture: a thin dark outline separates the words from whatever is behind them, the way a subtitle on a film does.

Keep it under about 2. The outline is painted *behind* the letterform rather than over it, so it thickens the shape without eating into it — but past a certain weight it closes up the gaps in letters like e and a.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOutlineWidth.label: Outline Thickness
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOverflow.hint:
What to do with contents too big for the room this has — which only happens if you have limited its width or height above.

"Let it spill out" lets the contents hang over the edges, ignoring the limit. "Cut it off" hides anything past the edge, cleanly but permanently — a reader has no way to see what was trimmed. "Let it scroll" puts a scroll bar on it so they can.

Cutting off is also what keeps a background picture inside rounded corners rather than poking out past them.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverOverflow.label: What Will Not Fit
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPaddingBottom.hint:
Empty space below the contents, on the INSIDE of its edge — the breathing room between the words and the border around them.

Without it, lettering sits right against the edge and looks cramped, the way text does when it runs to the very edge of a photocopy. Ten to sixteen is comfortable for a read-aloud box; a tight label might want three or four.

Not to be confused with outer spacing, which is the room *outside* the edge.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPaddingBottom.label: Bottom Padding

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPageButtonBorderBot:
What colour the bottom button edge line is drawn in.

A line that is only slightly darker than the surface it sits on reads as a fold or a crease; one in a strong contrasting colour reads as a deliberate frame. Both are useful — just pick one on purpose.

What kind of line the bottom button edge is drawn as — solid, dashed, dotted, double, or one of the ridged and grooved kinds that try to look three-dimensional.

Solid is right nearly always. Dashed reads as a cut-out or a note to be filled in; double suits a formal frame around a title. The ridged ones come from very old web design and rarely look good on a printed-page style.

How thick the bottom button edge line is, in pixels. 0 means no line at all on that side.

You do not have to draw all four. One thick line down the left side and nothing anywhere else is the classic look for a read-aloud box, and it is quieter than a full frame.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPageButtonCornerBot:
How far the bottom-left corner of the button is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.

How far the bottom-right corner of the button is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPageButtonCornerSha:
What kind of cut the corners of the button are given. They all use the four sizes set above — this only changes the shape of the cut.

"Rounded" is the ordinary curve everyone expects. "Bevel" cuts the corner off flat, like a mitred picture frame or a cut gemstone — good for anything meant to look built rather than printed. "Notch" cuts a square step out of it. "Scoop" curves inward instead of outward, which makes a box look like a stamped seal or a torn ticket.

If nothing changes when you pick one, the corner sizes above are still 0 — there is no cut yet for this to shape.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPageButtonInnerShad:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Leave it at 0 unless you have a reason. A little negative — say -2 — pulls the shadow in so it peeks out only on one side, which is a neat way to get a subtle lift without a dark halo all the way round.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPageButtonSize.hint: How large the edit pencil is.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPictureCrop.hint:
What to do when the picture is not the shape you asked for above.

"Crop to fill" scales it up until it covers the whole shape and trims whatever hangs over — the picture stays undistorted, but you lose the edges. "Fit whole inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave empty bands at the sides. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, which makes faces look wrong and is almost never what you want.

Cropping is the usual choice. Use Which Part Is Kept below to decide what survives the trim.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPictureCrop.label: How It Fills The Shape
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPictureFrom.hint:
When a picture is cropped, this says which part of it to keep.

It matters most for portraits: crop a tall picture to a wide shape from the middle and you often behead the subject. Anchor it to the top instead and you keep the face.

Only does anything when a Picture Shape is set and the picture is being cropped to fill it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPictureFrom.label: Which Part Is Kept
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPictureShape.hint:
Crops every picture wearing this treatment to the same shape, whatever shape it started as.

This is what makes a page look composed rather than assembled. Half a dozen portraits pulled from different places will all be different shapes; set them all to Square, or all to Widescreen, and they suddenly look like they belong to the same book.

Leave it alone and each picture keeps its own shape, which is what a journal does now.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPictureShape.label: Picture Shape
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPosition.hint:
Whether this sits wherever the page puts it, or sticks to the screen as the page scrolls past it.

"Held in view" is the interesting one: the thing scrolls along with everything else until it reaches the top of the page area, and then it stays there while the rest keeps going. A map or a stat box can follow the reader down a long section that refers back to it.

It needs Nudge Down set to something — that is the distance from the top it stops at. Left at 0 it sticks to the very top edge.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverPosition.label: How It Sits
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverQuoteColor.hint: Text color of a short quotation. Leave empty to follow the page.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverQuoteColor.label: Quotation Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverQuoteFont.hint: The typeface used for a short quotation.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverQuoteFont.label: Quotation Typeface
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverQuoteStyle.hint: Whether a short quotation is italic.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverQuoteStyle.label: Quotation Slant
The color behind a secret passage after it has been shown.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverRevealedTexture.hin:
A picture laid behind this — a parchment scan, a stone texture, a photograph.

Point it at any image in your Foundry data: your own art, artwork from a game system, or another module's. Leave it empty for no picture at all.

The picture sits *behind* the lettering on its own layer, so the controls under it — softness, brightness, strength — change the picture without touching the words in front of it.
Browns the picture, the way an old photograph or a sheet of paper yellows with age. 0 leaves its own colours; 100 is fully sepia.

A quick way to make a modern photograph belong on a fantasy page. Try it around 60 to 80 together with Image Colour turned down.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverRevealedTextureBlen:
How the picture mixes with the Fill Color behind it, rather than simply covering it up.

This is the trick that makes textures work, and it is worth learning one setting: **Multiply**. With a greyscale texture over a coloured fill, Multiply keeps every dark speck of the texture while letting the colour show through the light parts — so one grey parchment scan can be aged ivory on one style and cold slate on another, just by changing the Fill Color under it.

"Normal" means no mixing at all: the picture simply sits on top and the fill beneath it does nothing. Use that when the picture already has the colours you want.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverRevealedTextureBlur:
Blurs the picture before it is laid down behind the words.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverRevealedTextureBrig:
Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverRevealedTextureCont:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverRevealedTextureOpac:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverRevealedTexturePosi:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverRevealedTextureSatu:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverRowColor.hint: Background shared by every body row. Use a fully transparent color for none.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverRowColor.label: Row Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverScale.hint:
Draws this larger or smaller than the room it actually takes up on the page. 100 is its normal size.

Because the room it occupies does not change, going above 100 makes it overhang its neighbours rather than pushing them aside — which is how you get a picture that breaks out of its column, or a drop cap that spills into the margin.

Below 100 it shrinks and leaves a gap around itself. Small steps: 105 is noticeable, 150 is a lot.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverScale.label: Size

How far the bottom-left corner of the search box is cut away, in pixels. 0 leaves it a sharp right angle.

Small numbers — 2 to 6 — read as a printed panel with slightly worn corners. Large ones read as a modern app. Corners do not all have to match: rounding only the two right-hand corners is a neat way to make a box look like a tab or a bookmark.

The Corner Shape control below decides *what* the cut looks like — this only says how big it is.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchCornerShape.h:
What kind of cut the corners of the search box are given. They all use the four sizes set above — this only changes the shape of the cut.

"Rounded" is the ordinary curve everyone expects. "Bevel" cuts the corner off flat, like a mitred picture frame or a cut gemstone — good for anything meant to look built rather than printed. "Notch" cuts a square step out of it. "Scoop" curves inward instead of outward, which makes a box look like a stamped seal or a torn ticket.

If nothing changes when you pick one, the corner sizes above are still 0 — there is no cut yet for this to shape.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchInnerShadowBl:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchInnerShadowCo:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchInnerShadowOf:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.

Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchInnerShadowSp:
Inner shading is a shadow cast *inside* the edges, so the surface looks slightly sunken — pressed into the page rather than sitting on top of it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Leave it at 0 unless you have a reason. A little negative — say -2 — pulls the shadow in so it peeks out only on one side, which is a neat way to get a subtle lift without a dark halo all the way round.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchPlaceholderCo: Color of the grayed-out prompt shown while the search box is empty.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchSize.label: Text Size
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchTexture.hint:
A picture laid behind this — a parchment scan, a stone texture, a photograph.

Point it at any image in your Foundry data: your own art, artwork from a game system, or another module's. Leave it empty for no picture at all.

The picture sits *behind* the lettering on its own layer, so the controls under it — softness, brightness, strength — change the picture without touching the words in front of it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchTexture.label: Background Image
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchTextureAge.hi:
Browns the picture, the way an old photograph or a sheet of paper yellows with age. 0 leaves its own colours; 100 is fully sepia.

A quick way to make a modern photograph belong on a fantasy page. Try it around 60 to 80 together with Image Colour turned down.
How the picture mixes with the Fill Color behind it, rather than simply covering it up.

This is the trick that makes textures work, and it is worth learning one setting: **Multiply**. With a greyscale texture over a coloured fill, Multiply keeps every dark speck of the texture while letting the colour show through the light parts — so one grey parchment scan can be aged ivory on one style and cold slate on another, just by changing the Fill Color under it.

"Normal" means no mixing at all: the picture simply sits on top and the fill beneath it does nothing. Use that when the picture already has the colours you want.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchTextureBlur.h:
Blurs the picture before it is laid down behind the words.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchTextureBright:
Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchTextureContra:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchTextureFit.hi:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchTextureOpacit:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchTexturePositi:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSearchTextureSatura:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarAlign.hi: Which edge the settings line up against on the strip.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarBackgrou: The color behind the strip the page's settings stand on.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarBorderBo:
What colour the bottom strip edge line is drawn in.

A line that is only slightly darker than the surface it sits on reads as a fold or a crease; one in a strong contrasting colour reads as a deliberate frame. Both are useful — just pick one on purpose.

What kind of line the bottom strip edge is drawn as — solid, dashed, dotted, double, or one of the ridged and grooved kinds that try to look three-dimensional.

Solid is right nearly always. Dashed reads as a cut-out or a note to be filled in; double suits a formal frame around a title. The ridged ones come from very old web design and rarely look good on a printed-page style.

How thick the bottom strip edge line is, in pixels. 0 means no line at all on that side.

You do not have to draw all four. One thick line down the left side and nothing anywhere else is the classic look for a read-aloud box, and it is quieter than a full frame.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarFont.hin: The lettering on the strip. Each setting standing on it follows this unless it is given a typeface of its own.
Whether a long word may be split across two lines with a hyphen, the way a printed book does it.

It matters in narrow columns. Without hyphenation, one long word that will not fit gets pushed to the next line and the browser stretches the gaps on the line before to compensate — you end up with rivers of white space running down the page. Letting it hyphenate keeps the spacing even.

Worth turning on for anything set in columns or in a narrow box; unnecessary for full-width paragraphs, where there is room to breathe.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarLetterSp: Extra space between the letters on the strip.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarLineHeig: How tall each row on the strip is. 0 follows the window.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarMarginBo:
Empty space below this, on the OUTSIDE of its edge — the room between it and whatever else is on the page.

This is the one people mix up with padding, so: outer spacing pushes other things away, inner spacing pushes its own contents in. If a box is crowding the paragraph above it, this is the control you want.

A negative number pulls it closer instead, which lets a box overlap what is above or below it — occasionally what you want for a heading that should sit over a banner.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarOutlineC:
What colour the outline around each letter is drawn in.

Only shows if the Outline Thickness above is more than 0. A colour close to the page's own background works best — the outline is meant to hold the letters apart from what is behind them, not to be noticed itself.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarOutlineW:
Draws a line around the outside of each letter, in pixels. 0 for none.

This is how you make pale lettering readable on top of a busy background picture: a thin dark outline separates the words from whatever is behind them, the way a subtitle on a film does.

Keep it under about 2. The outline is painted *behind* the letterform rather than over it, so it thickens the shape without eating into it — but past a certain weight it closes up the gaps in letters like e and a.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarPaddingB:
Empty space below the settings on the strip, on the INSIDE of its edge — the breathing room between the words and the border around them.

Without it, lettering sits right against the edge and looks cramped, the way text does when it runs to the very edge of a photocopy. Ten to sixteen is comfortable for a read-aloud box; a tight label might want three or four.

Not to be confused with outer spacing, which is the room *outside* the edge.

This is the single most useful control here. A photograph or a scan at full sharpness competes with the text sitting on top of it and makes it hard to read. Blur it by 3 or 4 and it stops being a picture you look at and becomes a texture you look past — which is what a background is for.

Makes the picture lighter or darker before it is laid down. 100 leaves it alone; below 100 darkens it, above 100 lightens it.

Which way you go depends on your text. Dark lettering needs a pale background, so push a busy texture up to 130 or so until the words sit clearly on top. Pale lettering needs the opposite — down to 60 or 70, until the page can hold light ink.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarTextureC:
How big the gap is between the picture's lightest and darkest parts. 100 leaves it alone, lower flattens it towards a single flat grey, higher makes the darks darker and the lights lighter.

Lowering it is usually what you want for a background. A parchment scan at 40 keeps just enough grain to read as paper without any one blotch pulling the eye.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarTextureF:
What to do when the picture is not the same shape as the area it has to fill.

"Tile" repeats it like wallpaper, which is what you want for a seamless texture such as paper grain or stone. "Fill the area" scales it up until it covers everything, cropping whatever hangs over the edges — right for a photograph. "Fit inside" shrinks it until all of it shows, which may leave gaps. "Stretch" squashes it to fit exactly, and usually looks it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarTextureO:
How strongly the picture shows through. 100 is the picture at full strength, 0 hides it entirely.

Because the picture is on its own layer behind the words, turning this down fades the picture without fading the lettering. Somewhere between 15 and 40 is usually right for a texture that is meant to be felt rather than noticed.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarTextureP:
Which part of the picture to keep when it is bigger than the area, or where to anchor it when it is smaller.

It matters most with "Fill the area", where something always gets cropped. If the interesting part of your picture is at the top — a sky, a castle — anchor it to the top so that is the part that survives.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarTextureS:
How much colour the picture keeps. 100 leaves it as it is; 0 drains it to grey.

Draining it is worth trying even when you want a colourful page. Set this to 0 and then tint the picture with the Fill Color underneath it using Multiply blending — you get the texture of the photograph with a colour you chose, rather than whatever colour the photograph happened to be.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarWordSpac: Extra space between the words on the strip.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSettingsBarWrap.hin:
Lets the browser be cleverer about where the lines break, instead of simply filling each one until it runs out of room.

"Even up the lines" is for headings. A two-line heading normally comes out with eight words on the first line and one on the second; this balances them so both lines are about the same length, which looks deliberate rather than accidental.

"Avoid a lone last word" is for paragraphs. It stops a paragraph ending with a single word stranded on its own line — printers call that an orphan, and once you notice it you cannot stop noticing it.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverShadowBlur.hint:
A shadow is what makes something look raised off the page rather than printed flat on it. This is how fuzzy its edge is. 0 gives a hard-edged shape, like a shadow in bright noon sun; a larger number spreads it into a soft haze, like an overcast day.

If a shadow looks fake, this is usually the reason. Real shadows are softer the further the thing sits from what it falls on, so a small offset wants a small softness to match.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverShadowBlur.label: Softness
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverShadowColor.hint:
A shadow is what makes something look raised off the page rather than printed flat on it. This is what colour it is painted.

Pure black almost always looks wrong. Real shadows take a colour from what they fall on, so on a warm parchment page a dark brown reads far better than black. Turn the opacity down too — somewhere around 25% to 40% is usually plenty.

Set the colour fully transparent and there is no shadow at all, which is how you switch one off.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverShadowColor.label: Color
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverShadowOffsetX.hint:
A shadow is what makes something look raised off the page rather than printed flat on it. This is how far it slides to the right, in pixels. A negative number slides it left instead.

Think of it as where the light is standing. Light from the left throws the shadow right, so a positive number here and a positive Vertical Offset together read as a lamp up and to the left — which is what most people expect, and what almost every printed book uses.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverShadowOffsetX.label: Horizontal Offset
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverShadowOffsetY.hint:
A shadow is what makes something look raised off the page rather than printed flat on it. This is how far it slides down, in pixels. A negative number lifts it up instead.

Keep it small. Two or three pixels reads as paper lying on a table; twenty reads as a sticker floating an inch above it, which is rarely what you want on a page people are meant to read.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverShadowOffsetY.label: Vertical Offset
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverShadowSpread.hint:
A shadow is what makes something look raised off the page rather than printed flat on it. This grows or shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it can be bigger or smaller than the thing casting it.

Leave it at 0 unless you have a reason. A little negative — say -2 — pulls the shadow in so it peeks out only on one side, which is a neat way to get a subtle lift without a dark halo all the way round.
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverShadowSpread.label: Size
ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverShown.hint: Whether the journal's name is drawn above the page at all.

ILLUMINUS.Field.hoverSize.hint:
